Lesson plan: Your AI Toolkit

How to ask AI good questions, check its answers, learn honestly with it, and keep growing your skills.

By the end of the lesson, students can

  • write a good prompt with a role, context, a clear task, an example and a format;
  • check an AI answer: open the sources, compare with trusted ones, and notice when it sounds too sure;
  • use AI as a tutor, not a ghostwriter, and explain why doing the thinking yourself matters.

Warm-up

What could AI help you with in your homework, and what should it never do for you?

Collect both lists on the board. Keep them: they are the start of your class rules at the end of the lesson.

Reading

Students read the lesson “Your AI Toolkit”. Students look for the five ingredients of a good prompt, three warning signs in an answer, and the difference between a tutor and a ghostwriter.

Activity: Mini-lab “Prompt makeover”

  1. Students open the mini-lab in lesson 12: a vague prompt, “Tell me about volcanoes.”
  2. They add the ingredients one at a time and, after each one, note what changed in the answer and on the quality meter.
  3. They take the ingredients out one at a time to find which one changes the answer most.
  4. Pairs write a five-ingredient prompt of their own for a topic from another subject.

For students who finish early

Fast finishers turn a ghostwriter prompt (“Write my essay about volcanoes”) into a tutor prompt that asks for hints and feedback instead.

Discussion questions

  • Asking a chatbot “Are you sure?” isn't a real check. Why not?
  • Where is the line between getting help and cheating? Does it depend on the task?
  • Why does working things out yourself, even with mistakes, help you remember?
  • Which human skills will matter most in a future with AI? Why?

Exit ticket

Write a tutor prompt for something you are stuck on in another subject.

Quick check. You're stuck on a maths homework problem. What is the best way to use AI?
Right answer: Ask for a hint or the method, then solve it yourself

Easier and harder

Easier. Give the five ingredients as sentence starters: “You are…”, “I am… and I need it for…”, “Explain…”, “For example…”, “Answer as…”.

Harder. Give students a printed chatbot answer that you prepared, with a few claims in it. They check it against two trusted sources and mark every claim as confirmed, wrong or not found.
